newsitem.title: UK: N. Ireland awaits Loyalist response to IRA attack.
newsitem.headline: N. Ireland awaits Loyalist response to IRA attack.

text.p: Northern Ireland's Roman Catholics and Protestants waited anxiously on Thursday to see whether pro-British guerrillas would take revenge for an IRA bombing that injured 31 people.
Protestant leaders implored "Loyalist" guerrilla groups not to retaliate to Monday's attack on the British Army's headquarters in Northern Ireland.
"I think what we've got to do is let the provos (IRA) commit hara kiri," said David Ervine, of the Progressive Unionist Party, political wing of the banned Ulster Volunteer Force.

Loyalist guerrillas were reported to be planning to meet in the next few days. Their long silence has left the province wondering whether it will be thrown back into the 25-year civil war between Protestants fighting to keep British rule and Roman Catholics seeking unification with Ireland.
The IRA set off two bombs at the garrison at Lisburn, 10 miles (15 km) south of Belfast, in an attack described by police as "a deliberate attempt at mass murder."

It was the republican guerrilla group's first attack in the province since it called a ceasefire in August 1994. It retracted the truce on February 9 this year when it launched the first of a series of bombings on the British mainland.

Northern Irish police said the attack was probably planned at least four months ago, when the peace talks sponsored by Britain and Ireland were just beginning. One of the cars used in the attack was bought in June.
The two bombs went off 20 minutes apart, apparently so that rescue services and people injured in the first blast would be caught by the second, planted outside a medical centre.
"They wanted to create the maximum amount of death and threat to life by the way they strategically placed the cars," said Detective Chief Superintendent Derek Martindale.

The IRA has denied Loyalist charges that it was trying to draw its Protestant rivals into renewed conflict, saying the attack was intended to put pressure on Britain to allow its political arm, Sinn Fein, into the peace talks.
Sinn Fein has been prohibited from taking part until the IRA hands over its weapons and declares a new truce.
Protestant leaders urged the British government to respond with tighter security and sanctions against Sinn Fein.

"I think there needs to be a response and the sooner that response comes the better. We need something that's going to give confidence to the people of the province," said David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, after meeting British Prime Minister John Major in Bournemouth, England.
Security has already been tightened across Northern Ireland after two years of peace. On Wednesday, British soldiers returned to patrolling the border crossings with Ireland.
Ireland's parliament, shaken by this week's attack, has called a full-day debate on Thursday on the precarious Northern Ireland peace process.
Both sides are expected to stress that the republic will not tolerate violence for political ends.
Irish Prime Minister John Bruton has accused the IRA of a "cynical betrayal" of peace efforts and of resorting to the type of tactics used by fascists.
Opposition leader Bertie Ahern said the IRA had "broken faith."
"They are wrong and will never achieve anything by going back to the bomb and bullet," said Ahern.
